passage:
The bedroom door slammed so hard in the Madrid apartment that a photo fell off the hallway wall. 'You never let me do ANYTHING!' Leila shouted through it, because Rafael had said no to the midnight concert.
Rafael stood in the hallway, picking up the glass. His chest was tight. He felt like a doormat and a villain at the same time.
He didn't shout back. He knocked once and spoke to the door. 'I can hear you're really angry. Slamming isn't okay, because things break. I'm here when you're ready.'
Forty minutes later Leila came into the kitchen, eyes puffy. 'Sorry about the photo.'
Rafael made two hot chocolates. 'Now tell me about the concert. Properly.' He listened. The answer was still no, but together they found a Saturday afternoon show instead.

qa.q: What fell off the hallway wall?
qa.a: A photo fell off the hallway wall when the door slammed.

qa.q: How did Rafael feel standing in the hallway picking up the glass?
qa.a: He felt tense and torn, his chest tight, as if he were a doormat and a villain at the same time.

qa.q: What choice did Rafael make that held the limit and kept connection?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named Leila's anger, said slamming isn't okay, and waited to talk properly over hot chocolate once Leila had settled.

qa.q: How might Leila feel when Rafael still says no but helps find another show?
qa.a: Leila may still be disappointed but feel heard and respected, since he listened properly and offered a real alternative.

grounding: Shows an adult facing a teenager's slammed door and outburst, staying calm, holding a limit on behaviour and talking after feelings settle.

passage:
On parents' day at the school, Darshan had taken leave from his shop job to come, because Ma was on night shift. The class teacher had barely said 'maths has dropped' when Mridul shoved back his chair, shouted, 'Everyone's always on my case!' and stormed into the corridor, kicking a bench on the way.
Darshan felt heat rise in his face. He had given up a day's pay for this.
He followed and kept his voice low. 'You can be angry. You can't kick things or yell at your teacher. Sit here with me till you're ready.'
Mridul stared at the noticeboard for ten minutes. Then, quietly: 'I'm scared I'll fail, bhaiya.'
In the canteen afterwards, over two samosas, they talked properly. Then Darshan walked him back in to apologise to the teacher.

qa.q: Why had Darshan taken leave from his shop job?
qa.a: Because Ma was on night shift, so he came to parents' day.

qa.q: What did Darshan feel when Mridul stormed out, and why?
qa.a: He felt heat rise in his face, hurt and taken for granted, since he had given up a day's pay to be there.

qa.q: What choice did Darshan make that held a limit and kept connection?
qa.a: He stayed calm, said anger is fine but kicking and yelling aren't, sat with Mridul till he settled, and then talked over samosas.

qa.q: What might Mridul's outburst have been hiding?
qa.a: Fear: Mridul admitted being scared of failing, which came out as anger at everyone being on his case.

grounding: Shows an older brother facing a teenager's outburst, feeling walked on, yet staying calm, holding a limit and talking once feelings settle.

passage: In their small house in Malerkotla, Yusuf, nineteen, was studying for an exam when Noor, fifteen, came home and hurled her school bag across the room. "I hate that school! I hate everyone!" The bag knocked his books to the floor. Yusuf felt the old heat: she always did this, walked all over everyone. He wanted to shout back. Instead he picked up his books slowly. "You're angry, I get it. But you don't throw things at me." She stormed up to the roof. He let her be. Half an hour later he carried two glasses of lassi up the stairs. She was crying. "Want to tell me?" he asked. She did.

qa.q: What did Yusuf carry up to the roof?
qa.a: Two glasses of lassi.

qa.q: What did Yusuf feel when the bag hit his books?
qa.a: He felt angry and walked over, wanting to shout back.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that kept the connection with Noor?
qa.a: He set a calm limit on throwing things, gave her space and then offered lassi and a chance to talk.

qa.q: How was Noor feeling by the time Yusuf reached the roof?
qa.a: Noor was sad and crying under the anger, ready to talk.

grounding: Illustrates a sibling facing a teen's outburst who stays calm, holds a limit and reconnects once feelings settle.

passage: When Gabriel said no to the concert in Madrid, fifteen-year-old Omar exploded. "You never let me do anything!" He kicked a kitchen chair across the floor and slammed his bedroom door so hard the glass in the hallway rattled. Gabriel stood in the kitchen of their Lisbon flat, hands shaking. He felt like a punching bag in his own home. He wanted to go and bang on the door. He didn't. He picked up the chair and texted: "I love you. The concert answer is still no. Kicking furniture is not okay. Let's talk after dinner." At eight Omar came out, eyes red. They talked for an hour, and Gabriel listened more than he spoke.

qa.q: What did Omar kick across the floor?
qa.a: A kitchen chair.

qa.q: How did Gabriel feel after the door slammed?
qa.a: He felt shaken and hurt, like a punching bag in his own home.

qa.q: Why was Gabriel's text a wise response?
qa.a: It showed love, kept the limit on the concert and on kicking furniture, and set a time to talk once feelings settled.

qa.q: How might Omar feel coming out at eight?
qa.a: Omar seems upset and tired, red-eyed, but ready to talk.

grounding: Shows a parent facing a teen's outburst who stays calm, holds limits and reconnects after feelings settle.

passage:
The hostel common room at the girls' boarding school was full on visiting Sunday. Rekha had brought her younger sister Sarita's favourite snacks.
Within ten minutes Sarita had flung the packet on the floor. "You never listen! You told Mummy about my marks!" She stormed off and slammed the dormitory door so hard the warden looked up.
Rekha sat very still, face hot, feeling everyone's eyes on her. Part of her wanted to leave and not come back next month.
The warden came over. "Give her a little time. She's allowed to be angry, not to throw things."
Twenty minutes later Sarita came back, eyes red. Rekha picked up the packet. "I'm not okay with things being thrown. But I'm listening now. Tell me why the marks thing hurt." Sarita sat down beside her and, slowly, began to talk.

qa.q: What did Sarita throw on the floor?
qa.a: She flung the packet of snacks Rekha had brought on the floor.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling after the door slammed?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt, her face hot, and part of her wanted to leave and not come back next month.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Rekha, and why?
qa.a: She stayed calm, held a clear limit about throwing and waited until Sarita settled before talking, which kept them connected.

qa.q: Why might Sarita react so strongly to her marks being shared?
qa.a: She may feel exposed and betrayed that Rekha told Mummy, and her feelings come out in one big burst.

grounding: Rekha faces her teenage sister's slammed door and outburst, stays calm, holds a limit on behaviour and talks once feelings settle.
